newsitem.title: USA: Republicans outline "budget accord" with Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Republicans outline "budget accord" with Clinton.

text.p: Congressional Republican leaders presented to party colleagues the outlines of a balanced budget accord with Democratic President Bill Clinton on Thursday and said they hope to put the finishing touches on the historic plan later in the day.
A closed-door meeting of Republicans erupted in cheers after leaders explained the outlines of a proposal to balance the federal budget by 2002 and give many Americans a tax cut.

Representative Marge Roukema of New Jersey told reporters House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich "indicated that it should be finalised this afternoon." Republican Whip Tom DeLay said he expected conservative Democrats would support the plan.

But at the White House, administration officials insisted at midday that no final agreement had been reached. And Clinton's Democrats complained they had been left in the dark on the details. "I don't know the details, my sources are all in the White House," said one House Democratic aide sarcastically.
"There's no agreement," said one administration official. "There's still important issues that have not been resolved yet," he added.
Another administration official said that the unresolved issues included Medicare, taxes and non-defence spending, all issues important to win backing of Democrats.
Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, Democrat of South Dakota, said he was concerned about the magnitude of tax cuts under discussion and the "limited" investment for education.

But Roukema, who said Republicans were cautioned not to call it "a budget deal" but to refer to it as "an accord," told reporters, "It seems as though there is an enormous amount of agreement across the board on the budget."

Republican sources said the budget accord would include a five-year gross tax cut of $135 billion. But Ways and Means Committee chairman Bill Archer, Republican of Texas, said the tax cut number was not final. Asked whether a net tax cut of $85 billion over five years was under discussion, Archer said that was one of the figures under discussion.
Medicare spending would be reduced by $115 billion over the five years. Spending cuts for domestic programmes had not been settled, the sources said.
The Democratic White House and Republican Congress have been at loggerheads over the budget since Republicans won majority control of both U.S. legislative chambers in 1994.

Gingrich and his conservative Republican allies came to power with the aim of slashing taxes and forcing the White House to accept deep cuts in the federal government. The budget battle led to two unpopular government shutdowns which the public generally blamed on Republicans.
The two sides fought to a stalemate in the U.S. elections last November -- Clinton returned triumphant to the White House and Republicans retaining their majorities in Congress.
This year they resumed negotiations with a determination to balance the budget by 2002. In recent weeks, both sides have shown new flexibility and willingness to compromise.

Republican conference chairman John Boehner of Ohio praised the White House this time around. "They dealt with us much more openly and much more honestly than what we went through two years ago," he told reporters .
But Democrats complained they had been left out.
Senate Democratic leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota was blunt. "This process stinks," he said of the closed door negotiations between the White House and Republicans.
Asked if he could support it, Daschle replied, "I don't know." He said he wanted to see more details before deciding.

The top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, Representative David Obey of Wisconsin, said if the budget agreement were as described to him, liberal Democrats would be "clamoring" to try to defeat it.
At least one conservative Republican, Sen. Phil Gramm of Texas, voiced his opposition to the plan.
"The American people will not get fiscal restraint, a better economy, a balanced budget or permanent tax relief," he said of the emerging agreement.
